Name: Priya Sharma
Education Level: Junior College / Pre-University
GPA: 3.85

Subjects:
Mathematics
Additional Mathematics
Physics
Computing

Extracurriculars:
- President of school's Computing & Robotics Club (2 years)
- Placed 3rd nationally in the Singapore National Olympiad in Informatics (NOI)
- Built and open-sourced a study-scheduling web app used by 300+ students across 3 junior colleges
- Volunteer coding instructor for a weekend program teaching Scratch to primary school students
- Represented school at the National STEM competition, won Merit award for a water-quality sensor project

Essay:
When I was fourteen, I taught myself Python by rewriting a broken attendance spreadsheet macro that our
CCA teacher-in-charge had given up on. That small fix turned into a habit: I now look for the clumsy,
manual processes around me and ask whether code could do it better. Leading my school's Computing Club
taught me that the hardest part of a project is rarely the algorithm — it's convincing five other people
to agree on a data model at 9pm before a deadline. Competing in NOI pushed me to think about efficiency
not as an afterthought but as a design constraint from the very first line of code. I want to study
Computer Science at NUS because I am drawn to the intersection of systems programming and applied AI,
and because Singapore's tech ecosystem gives me a direct path from classroom ideas to real deployed
products. Beyond the degree, I want to keep building tools that quietly remove friction from students'
lives, the same way that first spreadsheet fix did for my CCA.

questions: Why do you want to study Computer Science at NUS?
Describe a challenge you have overcome.
answers:
The first time I felt the specific thrill of computer science was at 2am, staring at a
segmentation fault in a pathfinding algorithm I had written for a school robotics competition.
I had modeled our warehouse-navigation robot's map as a grid, but a single off-by-one error in
my boundary check meant the robot occasionally tried to plan a path through a wall. Fixing that
one line taught me more about how computers actually "think" than a semester of lectures could
have. Since then I have built a Discord bot that automated attendance-tracking for my CCA of 80
members, cutting our weekly admin time from 45 minutes to under 5, and a small Android app that
helps my grandmother's neighborhood watch group log incidents in her first language. Both
projects left me wanting to understand the systems layer underneath the tools I was using —
how a database keeps data consistent under concurrent writes, how a compiler decides what code
is even valid. NUS's School of Computing draws me specifically because of the depth of its
systems and AI tracks and its proximity to Singapore's tech industry, which means the research
happening in its labs is often only a short bus ride from the companies applying it. I want to
spend the next four years moving from someone who patches bugs at 2am to someone who designs
the systems so those bugs are easier to catch in the first place.

Halfway through building the attendance bot I mentioned above, our CCA's exco unanimously voted
to scrap the project. They were worried that an unfamiliar tool would confuse the 60% of members
who barely used Discord beyond reading announcements, and a failed rollout right before our
annual showcase would embarrass the club. Rather than argue in the meeting, I asked for two
weeks to run a small pilot with just my own section of 15 members, and I promised to revert to
the old paper sign-in sheet immediately if it caused problems. During the pilot I sat with the
three members who were least comfortable with the tool and rebuilt onboarding around their
confusion points — mainly, they didn't know they needed to react to a message rather than type
a command. I rewrote the bot's welcome message around that single insight. When I brought the
pilot's 100% adoption rate and zero complaints back to the exco, they approved a full rollout.
The experience reshaped how I handle disagreement: instead of trying to win an argument with a
better pitch, I try to shrink the risk of being wrong down to something small enough that people
are willing to let me test it.

Dear Hiring Manager,

I'm writing to apply for the Software Engineering Intern role on the Payments Infrastructure
team at Stripe. I'm currently a third-year Computer Science student, and over the past year I've
worked on a few backend-focused projects, including a booking platform that automated
scheduling for a local business and reduced their manual admin work noticeably. I'm comfortable
with Python and JavaScript, and I've recently been learning Go because I'm interested in the
kind of distributed systems work Stripe is known for.

What draws me to Stripe specifically is the emphasis on developer experience — I've used the
Stripe API in a side project and was impressed by how clear the documentation and error messages
were compared to other payment providers I've tried. I'd like to contribute to that same quality
bar as an intern, whether that's on the API surface itself or the internal tooling that supports
it.

I've attached my resume, which goes into more detail on my projects and coursework. I'd welcome
the chance to talk more about how I could contribute to the team.

Sincerely,
Priya Sharma

interviewPlan.overview: Stripe is a global technology company that builds economic infrastructure for the internet. They focus on payment processing software and APIs for businesses, aiming to increase the GDP of the internet by simplifying complex financial transactions for companies of all sizes.
researchTips: Read the Stripe blog and engineering documentation to understand their technical culture and API-first philosophy.
Familiarize yourself with their product suite, such as Connect, Billing, and Radar, to see how they integrate with different business models.
Research their corporate values, particularly 'Move with urgency' and 'Trust is our product,' which are often discussed in their engineering literature.

technicalPrep: Review data structures and algorithms, focusing on API design and how to handle distributed systems at scale.
Practice coding in a language Stripe commonly uses, such as Ruby, Go, or Java, ensuring you can explain the trade-offs of your implementation.

interviewPlan.timelineAdvice: With 10 days left, spend the first 5 days on rigorous LeetCode-style practice and system design fundamentals, then use the remaining 5 days to rehearse behavioral answers and review the Stripe-specific product ecosystem.

commonQuestions.question: Tell me about yourself
commonQuestions.howToAnswer: Use the past-present-future model. Start with your current status, bridge to a concrete achievement, mention a team experience, and end with why Stripe is the natural next step.
commonQuestions.sampleAnswer: I am currently in my third year of Computer Science at my university, where I have developed a strong foundation in backend development and distributed systems. Last year, I led a project to build a custom real-time data processing pipeline that handled over 10,000 requests per minute during peak testing. Outside of my coursework, I served as the lead developer for our university's hackathon committee, which required coordinating technical requirements across a team of six developers. I have always been fascinated by how financial infrastructure can empower global commerce, which is why I have followed Stripe's engineering approach for years. Your emphasis on high-quality documentation and developer experience really resonates with my own coding philosophy. I am eager to apply my skills to solve complex integration challenges within your engineering team. My goal is to transition my academic knowledge into a professional environment that prioritizes scalable and reliable code.

commonQuestions.question: What is your greatest weakness?
commonQuestions.howToAnswer: Choose a real but non-fatal professional weakness and immediately follow up with the proactive steps you are taking to mitigate it.
commonQuestions.sampleAnswer: Sometimes I can be a bit too detail-oriented, which can slow me down during the initial phases of a project when speed is prioritized. I have realized that while precision is vital for backend systems, I need to balance it with the need for rapid prototyping. To manage this, I have started using time-boxing techniques to ensure I hit key milestones without getting stuck in the weeds. This allows me to maintain a high standard of quality while staying aligned with the team's broader delivery goals.

commonQuestions.question: What is your expected salary?
commonQuestions.howToAnswer: Acknowledge the research you have done for similar roles in the region and keep the focus on value, while providing a clear numerical range.
commonQuestions.sampleAnswer: Based on my research into software engineering internship roles in the region, the compensation for top-tier tech companies typically ranges from SGD 3,500–5,500 per month. I am certainly open to discussing the full benefits package and am primarily looking for a role that offers significant learning and mentorship opportunities within a high-growth team.

commonQuestions.question: Do you have any questions for us?
commonQuestions.howToAnswer: Ask insightful questions that show you have researched the team and care about their engineering culture.
commonQuestions.sampleAnswer: How does the engineering team balance the need for rapid feature deployment with the extreme requirement for 99.999% reliability in payment processing?

chatHistory.content: Which of my applications needs the most work right now?

Based on your current portfolio status, your **Cover Letter** for the Stripe internship is the priority. 

While your university application and resume are in great shape, your cover letter is currently the weakest link because it is too generic and doesn't leverage the impressive metrics you've already established in your resume.

Here is where you should focus your efforts:

*   **Quantify your impact:** In the cover letter, you mention your booking platform "reduced manual admin work noticeably." Swap this for the **80% reduction** you used on your resume. Concrete numbers signal professional maturity.
*   **Deepen the technical narrative:** Stripe values engineering depth. Don’t just say you are "learning Go"—mention a specific technical challenge you solved (e.g., handling concurrency or database consistency) that makes you a good fit for their **Payments Infrastructure** team.
*   **Address the international factor:** As an applicant from Kuala Lumpur, you need to proactively state your **work authorization** (e.g., your eligibility for a Singaporean student or training pass) to remove any hesitation a recruiter might have about your relocation logistics.

**Why the others can wait:**
*   **University (NUS):** Your profile is already highly competitive. You mainly need to perform final "polishing" (connecting your specific interests to NUS faculty or labs), which can be done in one sitting once you have time.
*   **Interview Prep:** You have a 10-day buffer. Use the next 48 hours to fix the cover letter, then shift your full attention to the Stripe-specific technical prep outlined in your plan. 

Would you like me to draft a revised paragraph for your Stripe cover letter using those metrics?

To make it more distinctively 'NUS,' replace the general mention of 'systems and AI tracks' with specific modules or faculty members whose research currently excites you. Demonstrating deeper research into the curriculum will show you are not just looking for a CS degree, but specifically an NUS education.

perQuestion.question: Describe a challenge you have overcome.
perQuestion.feedback: This is a mature and well-structured response that highlights soft skills like stakeholder management and empathy, which are vital for a software engineer. The resolution is highly effective because it focuses on a tangible process change rather than just a personality trait. You could further strengthen this by briefly reflecting on how this 'risk-shrinking' approach applies to your future aspirations in complex systems architecture.

feedback.summary: Priya demonstrates a highly competitive profile for the NUS Computer Science program, characterized by an excellent academic record and significant, high-level engagement in computing and robotics. Her performance at the National Olympiad in Informatics strongly aligns with the program's emphasis on algorithmic problem-solving and technical excellence.
strengths: GPA of 3.85 significantly exceeds the baseline requirement
Strong performance in competitive programming (NOI 3rd place)
Documented leadership experience as President of the Computing & Robotics Club
Tangible software development experience through open-source projects
High level of English proficiency confirmed by IELTS 8.0
gaps: Lack of advanced-level research or publications in CS to further differentiate from other top-tier applicants
Limited evidence of large-scale collaborative software projects beyond individual contributions
Need for a more cohesive narrative connecting the robotics and web development interests to a specific research area or professional goal
recommendations: Articulate a clear 'Statement of Purpose' that links your NOI experience and robotics projects to a specific research interest at NUS, such as AI or Systems.
Quantify the impact of your open-source web app (e.g., number of users, specific performance improvements) to demonstrate real-world utility.
Highlight any experience with complex software engineering practices, such as CI/CD, unit testing, or collaborative version control, in your personal statement.
Secure a strong recommendation letter from a mentor or teacher who can attest to your depth of technical reasoning and collaborative ability in a team setting.
feedback.internationalNote: As an international applicant, ensure that your academic transcripts are officially certified and clearly mapped to the local grading scales to facilitate a smooth equivalence assessment by the NUS admissions office.
